definition: Reconstruct means to build again after damage, or to piece together an understanding of past events from evidence.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reconstruct. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reconstruct should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Engineers worked through the winter to reconstruct the bridge the flood had washed away.
Repair is weaker than reconstruct, repairing fixes the damaged parts of something, while reconstructing builds the whole thing again.
Overhaul is stronger than reconstruct, reconstructing rebuilds what was damaged or lost, while an overhaul strips something down and redoes every part of it, even the parts that still worked.

Rebuild means to build a physical thing again after damage or destruction — you rebuild a bridge or an engine. Reconstruct covers that and one thing more: piecing together an account of past events from evidence, the way detectives reconstruct a timeline. You rebuild structures; you can reconstruct a night.

Restore means to return something to its original condition, often keeping the original materials — restorers work on paintings and old houses. Reconstruct means building the thing again, sometimes entirely from new parts, or assembling a picture of past events from clues rather than preserving anything original.

Reassemble means to fit existing pieces back together — the parts are all on the table and go back where they belong. Reconstruct starts with less: the original is damaged or gone and gets built again, or the past is pieced together from whatever scraps of evidence remain.

Reconstruct means to build again after damage, or to piece together an understanding of past events from evidence.
Using time-stamped receipts, doorbell-camera clips, and a parking stub, the detectives reconstructed the suspect's movements on the night of the theft.
The detectives never witnessed that night themselves.
They took separate scraps of evidence and fit them together into one coherent account of what happened, which is the evidence-based sense of reconstruct: rebuilding the past piece by piece.
Used both literally, as in reconstruct a building, and for evidence work, as in reconstruct events or reconstruct a timeline.

No plan of the merchant ship Meridian survived her sinking in 1758, and for two centuries she was only a name in port records.
Then divers found the wreck site: no hull to speak of, just ballast stones, scattered fittings, and a debris field the length of a soccer pitch.
From those fragments, a university team set out to reconstruct the vessel -- first on paper, then as a scale model.
The spacing of the ballast fixed the hull's width; the fittings dated the rigging; even the debris field's shape told them how she had broken apart.
Nothing original was repaired and nothing was put back together, because almost nothing remained.
The ship the visitors now walk through is an argument built from evidence.
